blocks.text: Since the other name of quails, سماني [sumānā], has plainly been given them from their fatness, as Bochart presently notes, ALB. Schultens, in Originib. Hebr. book 1, ch. 3, §39, p. 231, believes that these birds were also called שלו, سلوي [salwā], from that same quality; there he shows that the root سلي [s-l-y], שלה, also contains the notion of rich and fat. — HIOB Ludolf (in Commentar. ad Histor. Aethiop. on book 1, ch. 13, no. 96, p. 172, and in Adpend. ad Histor. Aethiop.), having come upon a passage of Porphyry, περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψυχῶν [peri apochēs empsychōn] book 1, §2, where he says that an army in Africa suffering from famine was saved by the arrival of locusts, contends that the שלוים are locusts. For it is well known that locusts are a very common food in almost the whole of the East. The Jews living in Arabia today also think that the שלוים are locusts, and Niebuhr himself agrees with them, Beschreib. von Arab. p. 172. But the strongest objection is that in the Arabic, Syriac and Chaldee dialects this word without any doubt means quails. Nor is שלו found among the names of locusts in Levit. XI, 22. More has been noted by I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 427, and Oedmann in the Vermischten Sammlungen vol. 4, ch. 6, p. 58. — That the שלוים are flying fish, met with in the Red Sea, which the inhabitants of those lands are also accustomed to eat (cf. Hasselquist p. 255; Niebuhr Beschreib. von Arab. p. 176; Forsskål Descriptt. Animal. p. 16), was formerly the conjecture of OL. RUDBECK (Ichthyol. Bibl. Specim. I.), which I. D. Michaelis elaborated further in his Commentat. super lege Mosaica Deut. XXII, 6. 7. §9, and in the Addition to §9, in Syntagm. Commentatt. vol. 2, p. 104 and 115; afterwards, however, he himself rejected it, and rightly so, since in the Red Sea there is no such abundance of flying fish that many thousands of people could be fed with them daily. Nor can these fish rise more than three or four feet above the sea. In addition, flying fish are not an ordinary food; rather, dried, they serve as a medicine for strengthening the stomach. Cf. Niebuhr p. 177. For other points see Faber and Oedmann, loc. cit. — The Seleucid birds [Turdus Seleucis Forsskål vol. 6 a, p. 5, no. 16, Arabic سمرمر [samarmar], Turdus roseus Linnaeus 2, p. 819, no. 15, 13th ed.; Oedmann 2, ch. 6, p. 103], whose coming (as Pliny reports, Hist. Nat. 10, ch. 26, sect. 39) the inhabitants of Mount Casius obtain by prayer from Jupiter when locusts are ravaging their crops; it has not been discovered where they come from or where they go, and they are never seen except when their protection is needed, were suspected by [II, 650] HERMANN VON DER HARDT to be the same as the שלוים; RATHLEF also fought for this opinion in his Append. Acridotheol., but with futile arguments, which I. D. Michaelis long ago refuted in the commentary cited, p. 104 ff. — There is a bird, common in Syria, Arabia and Egypt, of the size of a partridge or turtle-dove, of the grouse family, with hard and dry flesh, which the Arabs, from the call it utters, call قَطًّا [qaṭṭan] Katta (as Hasselquist and Russell write it) (see Golius's Lexic. p. 1934, where a description of this bird is also found); in Linnaeus it is Tetrao supra varius; rectricibus duabus intermediis duplo longioribus subulatis, see Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 754, no. 11, under the heading Alchata, where the synonyms and those who have treated of it are also listed. That this bird is the שלו of the Hebrews is so certain to Hasselquist that in his Travels p. 333, after describing it fairly accurately under the name Tetrao Israelitarum, he uses these words: this, if any, is the bird taken as food by the Israelites in the desert, since it is common in the places through which they wandered. But this very point holds also of the quail, and what is read of the שלוים in Moses does not fit any other bird, as we shall see in the following Chapter. — I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 442, thinks the Arabs' Katta is the same as the quail, though these birds are carefully distinguished by all who have written on the natural history of birds.
The Arabs' فُرْفُر [furfur] and فُرْفُور [furfūr] seem to agree with the Ethiopic word; Golius, in his Lexicon p. 1773, on the authority of Firuzabadi, says it is the name of some bird.

The ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] of Aristotle and Athenaeus is the Rallus alis rufo-ferrugineis of Linnaeus, or Crex (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 711), in French Roi de cailles, in German Wiesenschnarre or Wachtelkönig. At Alexandria this bird is today called سلوى [salwā], according to Niebuhr, p. 176, Descr. Arab. But I think that the Greek translators understood by ὀρτυγομήτραις [ortygomētrais] rather very large quails, which Bochart considers probable; read what follows from him.
